thread.title: Is Netflix Overvalued? Here's What Some Experts Think

author: Karl Kaufman
title: Is Netflix Overvalued? Here's What Some Experts Think
text:
Netflix stock has been on a remarkable run, gaining more than 150% over the past year and outpacing the rest of the so-called FAANG stocks. Though I've never invested in the company, I'm fascinated by its growth trajectory and wonder, like many others, if it's overvalued and if it still has room to run. First I spoke with Ed Lavery, Investment Specialist at SimilarWeb , who provided me with some data about international user growth in app installations. Here is his commentary:
"It was inevitable, but Netflix usage in the U.S. is being challenged by more players entering the market and stealing viewing time. This doesn't minimize their strength, but does speak to changing dynamics in the sector that require close monitoring.
To strengthen their overall offering, a big focus seems to be global diversification, with a major focus on emerging markets. Growth in Brazil looks like a real opportunity, while in developed ones, France is offering great prospects.
Out of Netflix's top markets, users in the U.K. are spending the longest per day streaming on app. In Argentina and Mexico, usage time is increasing at the fastest rate, having grown more than 45% year over year:
Netflix Q1 App Usage SimilarWeb
The number of U.S. Android devices with Netflix installed appears to have declined over the past 18 months. This could be a result of increasing competition from the likes of Amazon or Hulu, or it could be that more subscribers are streaming on devices such as TVs:
U.S. Android Devices With Netflix Installed Vs. Amazon Prime & Hulu SimilarWeb
The real key growth markets appear to be France and Brazil where installation has increased 106% and 69% respectively, Q1 vs Previous Year:
Percentage Growth Of International Android Devices With Netflix App Installed SimilarWeb
Next, I asked four investment experts for their take on the stock. They include:
Emmet Savage, CEO of Rubicoin, an educational investing app Daniel Lugasi, Portfolio Manager at VL Capital Management Dock David Treece, Financial Analyst at FitSmallBusiness.com JP Gravitt, Chief Market Strategist and CEO of Market Realist Is the stock overvalued? Is there room for growth?
Emmet Savage: Here’s a $170 billion company with a price to earnings over 250. It’s currently trading at 14 times price to sales and 42 times price to book. On the balance sheet there is over $6 billion in debt and there’s plenty more to come. Ask me to invest in that company, and I’m probably going to pass.
On the other hand, here’s a company that in two decades has completely revolutionised the way in which we produce, distribute, and consume content. It has over 120 million people paying a monthly membership fee. It’s helmed by a guy who came from nothing to create one of the most disruptive and influential forces the media world has ever seen.
Using traditional valuation methods, yes, Netflix is overvalued. It was overvalued 10 years ago at $5 a share. But Netflix isn’t a traditional business. This is a company that accounts for up to 35% of internet downstream traffic in the U.S. It has become integral to the lives of the millions who spend on average 90 minutes a day on it. For many, not having Netflix is akin to not having the internet.
Netflix is my largest holding by far and I believe it’s still in its early innings as a business. With over 4 billion broadband accounts around the world today, I think there’s plenty of room for this business to grow.
Daniel Lugasi: While many investors will focus on the sky-high P/E ratio of Netflix to determine whether the stock is overvalued, the better measure is to look at the company’s EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization) multiple vs its peers. Netflix is growing EBITDA at a pace that is over 3 times faster than its industry peers, which would justify a growth premium for the stock.
This premium that the stock commands incorporates both the potential for subscriber growth and the economies of scale that will benefit the company as subscribers reach critical mass relative to content costs.
From a fundamental perspective, traditional value investors would agree that Netflix’s stock is overvalued, but when one incorporates the upside growth risks, Netflix may be deserving of a premium if they can deliver on continued growth in the future while managing content costs.
Dock David Treece: At this point in the market cycle, Netflix, like much of the broader market, is extremely overvalued and has been for a while. However, because stock prices are based on public perception rather than sound financials, there’s still room for the stock to rise. What’s more, Netflix has increased its user base drastically over the last 12-24 months, putting it in a good position to increase revenue in as-yet unreported financials.
JP Gravitt: Netflix has been called overvalued for the last decade, so while a market cap of around $170 billion may seem steep for a company that is expected to do $16.1 billion in sales this year, it has been showing accelerated revenue growth since 2015. Investors are willing to pay very high valuations for acceleration.
However, the company will have to really beat expectations next year to keep propelling the stock up. Right now, revenue growth decelerates to 25% in 2019 from 38% in 2018. The stock will look overvalued as soon as the acceleration stops
How will the company’s debt load affect its continued expansion?
Savage: Netflix’s subscriber base, paired with the internal data that user base provides, should ensure debt incurred today will be used to fuel long-term expansion, not subdue it. The quality of the original content produced today will not only attract new subscribers through word of mouth, but the halo effect of award nominations and wins will make a subscription to Netflix a no-brainer for many.
Treece: Should Netflix’s revenue rise going forward, the company should be able to rearrange its long-term debt structure to finance continued expansion.
Gravitt: The company could pull back on spending if they wanted to and very easily raise equity. Investors would be more than willing to fund them going forward. Overall, debt is not really a worry here.
Lugasi: Debt has the potential to clamp down on the growth rate of Netflix as the company will need to continue issuing debt to fund their content costs. Currently, the company has approximately $8.5 billion in debt outstanding with the need to issue more in the future. As interest rates in the U.S. move up, this could cause further distress for the company as content costs balloon. This cash burn, combined with rising rates could spell trouble if subscriber growth tails off.
What about competition?
Gravitt: Amazon.com and Hulu are the first two that come to mind, but neither come close to Netflix in terms of content. Competitors have been ramping up their spending efforts to try and compete with Netflix for subscribers, but I think it's fair to say that Netflix is the favorite of consumers, while the other players are simply add-ons.
Though Amazon may seem the most obvious competition, Hulu may ultimately pose the most problems since they have a Hulu Live, supported by all the major networks with studios of their own.
Savage: One of Netflix’s great advantages in the early days was inept competition. That’s no longer the case, particularly with the likes of Walt Disney and Time Warner finally getting involved. But it’s not a zero-sum game by any means.
In under ten years, if things keep going the way they are, households will subscribe to anywhere between five and ten streaming services and will still be saving money relative to the cost of cable today. The real threat of increased competition will be the exacerbation of the already rich cost of content.
Netflix has already demonstrated pricing power, and with a growing user base, I believe those costs will be manageable.
Treece: Perhaps the biggest competition Netflix faces is from more traditional media companies which are scrambling to combine forces and compete in this new marketplace.
Lugasi: In terms of competition, the only true barrier to entry into the streaming video subscriber model is the need for capital. Netflix really lacks a moat around their business model, which will make it rather easy for large technology companies to challenge them in this space.
Amazon has been one of the most prominent competitive threats, but due to the fact that Prime Video is bundled with Prime subscriptions, it is not a truly standalone threat to Netflix.
The company that has the cash to launch a true, standalone competitor to Netflix is Apple . Apple could outright purchase Netflix , but it would be more likely that Apple replicates the success of Netflix with their own product offering, which would include original content. This would parallel the launch of Apple Music in many ways and it is the only logical next step for Apple in the streaming content wars.
Disclosure: The author and American Dream Investing own shares in DIS, AAPL and AMZN.
